title: Verify the Claim: Did poverty really rise across Philadelphia, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017?
text:
The article I am looking at is Alfred Lubrano’s “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty,” published by WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer on December 6, 2018.
The article compares poverty in Philadelphia between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. It gives several examples of neighborhoods where poverty apparently increased a lot, such as Eastwick, where the poverty rate went from 12% to 26%, and Holmesburg, where it went from 2% to 19%. In this assignment, I use census tracts to recreate the comparison and check whether the changes are large enough to be statistically meaningful.



I used two ACS variables for each Philadelphia census tract:
B07012_002: population below 100% of the poverty level B07012_001: total population for whom poverty status is determined
I calculated the poverty rate by dividing the proverty population by the total population of the tracts. I used these two variables because I need both the number of people in poverty and the total population to calculate the rate and its margin of error.



I used the ACS 5-year estimates for 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 because these are the same periods used in the article. I used the 5-year ACS rather than the 1-year ACS because the 1-year ACS is not available at the census-tract level. The 5-year estimates also give us tract-level data with margins of error.



The two periods do not overlap. The first period covers 2006–2010 and the second covers 2013–2017, so they do not share any survey years. I therefore treat the two estimates as independent when calculating the margin of error for the change.
If the two periods overlapped, the estimates would not be fully independent, so simply combining their margins of error would not be appropriate.



There are a few things I had to assume because the article does not explain them in detail.

I assume that “poverty rate” means the percentage of people below 100% of the federal poverty level.
The neighborhoods in the article, such as Eastwick and Holmesburg, are not Census geographies. Since the article does not explain exactly which census tracts were used, I use individual census tracts instead. Because of this, my numbers will not necessarily match the article exactly.
I assume the census tract boundaries are comparable between the two ACS periods, so I can match the same GEOID across the two periods.
The article does not state a confidence level for its comparisons. I use 90% confidence, which corresponds to a z-value of 1.645 and is the confidence level used for ACS published margins of error.



Show code
get_poverty <- function(yr) {

  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c(
      below_poverty = "B07012_002",
      total         = "B07012_001"
    ),
    state    = "PA",
    county   = "Philadelphia",
    year     = yr,
    survey   = "acs5",
    geometry = TRUE
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr)
    )
}

poverty_change <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2010),
  get_poverty(2017)
)


tract_geometry <- poverty_change %>%
  select(GEOID, geometry) %>%
  distinct(GEOID, .keep_all = TRUE)


poverty_wide <- poverty_change %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, period, estimate, moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = c(variable, period),
    values_from = c(estimate, moe)
  )

title: Verify the Claim: Did poverty really rise across Philadelphia, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017?
text:
Part 2 — Test

Step 1: Poverty rate and its margin of error
First, I calculated the poverty rate for each tract. Since the poverty rate is a proportion, I cannot just use the margin of error for the poverty count. I used moe_prop() to calculate the margin of error for the rate using the numerator, denominator, and their MOEs.


Show code
poverty_rate <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(

    
    poverty_rate_2006_2010 =
      `estimate_below_poverty_2006-2010` /
      `estimate_total_2006-2010` * 100,

    poverty_rate_2013_2017 =
      `estimate_below_poverty_2013-2017` /
      `estimate_total_2013-2017` * 100,

    
    poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 =
      moe_prop(
        `estimate_below_poverty_2006-2010`,
        `estimate_total_2006-2010`,
        `moe_below_poverty_2006-2010`,
        `moe_total_2006-2010`
      ) * 100,

    poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 =
      moe_prop(
        `estimate_below_poverty_2013-2017`,
        `estimate_total_2013-2017`,
        `moe_below_poverty_2013-2017`,
        `moe_total_2013-2017`
      ) * 100
  )




Step 2: Coefficient of variation and reliability
I also calculated the coefficient of variation (CV) for each poverty rate. I used the thresholds from Jurjevich et al. (2018): a CV below 12% is considered reliable, 12–40% is somewhat reliable, and above 40% is unreliable.
If the poverty rate cannot be calculated and the CV is NA, I leave the reliability result as NA instead of automatically calling it unreliable.


Show code
poverty_reliability <- poverty_rate %>%
  mutate(

    cv_2006_2010 =
      (poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645) /
      poverty_rate_2006_2010 * 100,

    cv_2013_2017 =
      (poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645) /
      poverty_rate_2013_2017 * 100,

    reliability_2006_2010 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2006_2010)  ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2006_2010 < 12    ~ "Reliable",
      cv_2006_2010 <= 40   ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                 ~ "Unreliable"
    ),

    reliability_2013_2017 = case_when(
      is.na(cv_2013_2017)  ~ NA_character_,
      cv_2013_2017 < 12    ~ "Reliable",
      cv_2013_2017 <= 40   ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                 ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )




Step 3: Change between periods, its margin of error, and the 90% test
I calculated the change in poverty rate by subtracting the 2006–2010 rate from the 2013–2017 rate. I then calculated the standard error and margin of error for this difference.
I used a 90% confidence level to test whether the change is statistically different from zero. In other words, if the absolute value of the z-score is greater than 1.645, I classify the change as significant.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_reliability %>%
  mutate(

    change_rate =
      poverty_rate_2013_2017 -
      poverty_rate_2006_2010,

    se_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_moe_2006_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_moe_2013_2017 / 1.645,

    se_diff  = sqrt(se_2006_2010^2 + se_2013_2017^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,

    z = change_rate / se_diff,

    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,

    direction = case_when(
      is.na(significant)            ~ NA_character_,
      significant & change_rate > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
      significant & change_rate < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE                          ~ "Not significant"
    )
  )




Show code
n_tract    <- nrow(poverty_tested)
n_na       <- sum(is.na(poverty_tested$significant))
n_tested   <- n_tract - n_na
n_sig      <- sum(poverty_tested$significant, na.rm = TRUE)
n_up       <- sum(poverty_tested$direction == "Significant increase", na.rm = TRUE)
n_down     <- sum(poverty_tested$direction == "Significant decrease", na.rm = TRUE)
n_notsig   <- n_tested - n_sig
pct_sig    <- round(100 * n_sig / n_tested)
pct_up     <- round(100 * n_up / n_tested)
pct_notsig <- 100 - pct_sig


valid_10 <- sum(!is.na(poverty_tested$reliability_2006_2010))
valid_17 <- sum(!is.na(poverty_tested$reliability_2013_2017))
pct_rel_10 <- round(100 * sum(poverty_tested$reliability_2006_2010 == "Reliable", na.rm = TRUE) / valid_10)
pct_rel_17 <- round(100 * sum(poverty_tested$reliability_2013_2017 == "Reliable", na.rm = TRUE) / valid_17)
pct_unrel_10 <- round(100 * sum(poverty_tested$reliability_2006_2010 == "Unreliable", na.rm = TRUE) / valid_10)
pct_unrel_17 <- round(100 * sum(poverty_tested$reliability_2013_2017 == "Unreliable", na.rm = TRUE) / valid_17)


How many tracts show a detectable change? Of 384 Philadelphia tracts, 376 can be tested. Only 63 (17%) show a change that is statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence (36 increases and 27 decreases). The other 313 (83%) are not distinguishable from zero: the estimated change could be sampling noise.
One thing to keep in mind is that I am using a 90% confidence level. Even if there were no actual changes, some tracts could still appear significant just because of sampling variation.

  count(direction) %>%
  mutate(direction = replace_na(direction, "No data (NA)")) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(direction = "Result of 90% test", n = "Number of tracts") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "How Many Tracts Show a Detectable Change in Poverty?",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia census tracts, ACS 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017"
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note("Test: |z| > 1.645 (90% confidence). MOE of the change = sqrt(MOE1^2 + MOE2^2).")

title: Verify the Claim: Did poverty really rise across Philadelphia, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017?
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
To check the article’s citywide number, I also added up all tracts (using moe_sum() for the counts, then moe_prop() for the rate).


Show code
city_check <- poverty_wide %>%
  summarise(
    below_10 = sum(`estimate_below_poverty_2006-2010`, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_10 = sum(`estimate_total_2006-2010`, na.rm = TRUE),
    below_17 = sum(`estimate_below_poverty_2013-2017`, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_17 = sum(`estimate_total_2013-2017`, na.rm = TRUE),
    moe_below_10 = moe_sum(`moe_below_poverty_2006-2010`, `estimate_below_poverty_2006-2010`, na.rm = TRUE),
    moe_total_10 = moe_sum(`moe_total_2006-2010`, `estimate_total_2006-2010`, na.rm = TRUE),
    moe_below_17 = moe_sum(`moe_below_poverty_2013-2017`, `estimate_below_poverty_2013-2017`, na.rm = TRUE),
    moe_total_17 = moe_sum(`moe_total_2013-2017`, `estimate_total_2013-2017`, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    rate_10 = below_10 / total_10 * 100,
    rate_17 = below_17 / total_17 * 100,
    moe_rate_10 = moe_prop(below_10, total_10, moe_below_10, moe_total_10) * 100,
    moe_rate_17 = moe_prop(below_17, total_17, moe_below_17, moe_total_17) * 100,
    change = rate_17 - rate_10,
    moe_change = sqrt(moe_rate_10^2 + moe_rate_17^2)
  )

city_r10 <- round(city_check$rate_10, 1)
city_r17 <- round(city_check$rate_17, 1)
city_chg <- round(city_check$change, 1)
city_moe <- round(city_check$moe_change, 1)


What the data supports
The article’s citywide figure of about 26% is close to my result. Summing the tracts gives a poverty rate of 25.7% in 2013–2017. The rate was 24.9% in 2006–2010, which is a change of 0.8 percentage points (±0.7).
The data also show that poverty increased in some parts of Philadelphia. 36 tracts (10% of the tracts that could be tested) had a statistically significant increase. So the article is picking up a real pattern, although the size of the change is not equally clear in every tract.
What the data does not show clearly
At the same time, the tract-level results do not show that poverty increased everywhere. 313 of 376 testable tracts (83%) do not have a statistically significant change. There are also 27 tracts with a statistically significant decrease.
This makes the article’s broader description of poverty “exploding” across “much of the city” harder to verify with the tract-level data. The data show increases in some places, but they also show many places where the change is not statistically distinguishable from zero.
The article also describes Eastwick as having the largest increase. I cannot confirm that from my tract-level analysis. The largest estimated changes have fairly large margins of error, and only 16 of the top 20 increases are statistically significant.
I also cannot use these data to say that Eastwick is now “much worse than during the depth of the downturn.” The 2006–2010 ACS is a five-year average, so it does not tell us exactly what happened during each year of the recession.
Cannot be determined.
Some of the article’s other claims cannot be checked with the data I used. For example, I cannot reproduce the poverty rates for Fairhill, Eastwick, Holmesburg, and Mayfair because the article does not explain which census tracts were included in each neighborhood.
I also did not have the race-specific poverty variables needed to check the article’s claims about poverty among white residents. The same problem applies to the median household income examples. In addition, I would need to know whether the dollar amounts in the article were adjusted for inflation.
Finally, the explanations in the article, such as opioids, an aging population, immigration, and evictions, cannot be tested using the poverty-rate variables alone. These factors might help explain changes in poverty, but this analysis does not provide evidence about their individual effects.
I did not attempt the optional neighborhood-aggregation extension.

title: Verify the Claim: Did poverty really rise across Philadelphia, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017?
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Original central paragraph: “In grim and startling detail, a new five-year federal survey of poverty in Philadelphia shows a city still not recovered from the Great Recession — with white poverty exploding, inequality becoming the norm, and an out-of-the-way neighborhood experiencing some of the worst ravages of privation.”
Rewrite:
Philadelphia’s poverty rate was about 25.7% in 2013–2017, compared with 24.9% in 2006–2010. Poverty increased significantly in 36 census tracts and decreased significantly in 27 tracts. However, most of the tracts that could be tested did not show a statistically significant change. This means that the increase in poverty was not the same across the whole city.
The data also show why we need to be careful with individual neighborhood comparisons. Some of the largest estimated changes have large margins of error, and I cannot confirm from the tract-level data that Eastwick had the largest increase. The ACS data can show where poverty rates were high and where some changes were large enough to be statistically significant, but they cannot tell us by themselves why those changes happened.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text: Chicago has long faced housing affordability challenges, and home prices vary considerably across the city’s neighborhoods. Understanding what drives these differences is essential to understanding the local housing market. In this project, we examine the factors influencing single-family home sale prices in Chicago from 2023 to 2025 and develop a predictive model to estimate prices for properties without recent sales. This model can help us explore how property characteristics, proximity to amenities, and location shape home values and provide insights into the challenges of equitable property assessment. We want to focus on the phenomena of “The Tax Divide,” meaning whether lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth (and are over-taxed) than expensive one in Chicago.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}


socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
Part 3: Final model

Building character:

Building size has a strong positive association with sale price: each additional square foot is associated with an estimated $316 increase in price.
Lot size is also positively associated with sale price.
Building age has a nonlinear relationship with price, as indicated by the positive squared-age coefficient and negative linear-age coefficient.
Bedroom count also matters: compared with the house that have 1-2 bedroom, homes with 3 bedrooms and 4–5 bedrooms have lower estimated prices, while homes with 6 or more bedrooms have higher estimated prices.



Spatial character:

Distance to the CBD has a significant negative coefficient, suggesting that homes farther from downtown tend to have lower prices.
Distance to outdoor seating also has a negative association with sale price, although the estimated effect is relatively small per unit of distance.
Crime counts within 500 feet are negatively associated with home prices.



Neighborhood socioeconomic characteristics:’

The percentage of residents with a bachelor’s degree has a nonlinear relationship with sale price: the linear coefficient is negative and the squared term is positive. This may reflect the fact that an area with a very high share of residents with a Bachelor’s degree may be areas where there are lots of graduate students, and therefore cannot afford to live in expensive housing.
Median neighborhood income and the percentage of residents aged over 64 are not statistically significant in this model. This may be because the community fixed effect accounts for these variables.



Community-level differences:

Many community fixed-effect coefficients are statistically significant. For example, Lincoln Park, Gold Coast, and Old Town have large positive coefficients relative to the omitted reference community, while several South and West Side communities have negative coefficients.

The Tax Divide
Although the residual map does not reveal a clear spatial pattern, we further examined whether prediction errors were associated with sale prices (low v. high prices). text:
Part 6: Reflection

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.

In our final model, the coefficient for the share of people over 64 is 141.9078 (β). Therefore for every 1% increase in the share of elderly people in a census tract, there is a $141.91 increase in predicted sale price of a home, holding all other variables constant.

Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

Our model’s findings are consistent with the Chicago Tribune’s investigation, which found that lower-value homes were assessed at a higher proportion of their actual value than more expensive homes. In our analysis, lower-value homes had an under/overvaluation ratio of 0.451, compared with 1.152 for higher-value homes. Nevertheless, we do not recommend that the Cook County Assessor adopt this model for property assessment, as further validation and evaluation of its potential biases are needed.
First, our final model is still off by $273,157.80. This is an immense range and can skew future assessments to either over- or under-value a home in drastically incorrect ways.
Second, while our final model does seem to address issues of spatial autocorrelation from our baseline model, it over-fixes by now under-valuing a much larger share of homes.
Third, these are both indications that we are “missing something” – either demographic, spatial, or some other metric – that would help better explain sale price. On the other hand, we may have included features that though they contributed to the overall RMSE, they may not actually be useful variables going forward. For example, distance to groceries did not lower the RMSE so much and so may not be worth including in future models.
Finally, while a tax assessment model may help people lower their taxes, if it is an open source government model, it could be used by for-profit real estate companies to “game the market” in order to aquire under-taxed homes. There is no such thing as no-strings-attached in the real estate market.

text:
What this means for policy
Address all three:

Which communities in your state do we know the least about? The ACS data suggest that we know the least about smaller communities in Florida, particularly Lafayette County and Liberty County. Lafayette County has the largest relative margin of error in my analysis, with a MOE of 8.82%, followed by Liberty County at 6.93%. In comparison, 43 of Florida’s 67 counties fall into my high-confidence category, while 19 are moderate and only 5 are classified as low confidence.
Why? This pattern is related to how the ACS is collected. Unlike a complete census, the ACS estimates population and housing characteristics from a sample of households. Smaller counties generally have fewer households and therefore fewer sampled households. With a smaller sample size, estimates are subject to greater sampling uncertainty, which can produce a larger margin of error relative to the estimate. My results illustrate this relationship: high-confidence counties have an average population of 352,728, while low-confidence counties have an average population of only 11,947.
What could go wrong? This uncertainty matters for public policy because agencies may treat all county-level estimates as equally precise. If funding were allocated based on occupied housing unit estimates without considering their uncertainty, smaller counties could be disadvantaged. Their estimates are less reliable, so policymakers might underestimate or overestimate their actual housing needs and allocate resources based on numbers that appear more certain than they really are.



Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.

This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
The feature that helped the most was the log-transformed drug density when it was combined with unemployment rate, median household income, and school-distance categories. The final model reduced CV RMSE from 9.63 for the baseline model to 8.99. In contrast, the original spatial-feature model had a higher CV RMSE of 10.57, so adding spatial variables does not automatically improve prediction. The drug variables may overlap with information already captured by unemployment and income, while the log transformation helped reduce the influence of tracts with very high drug-incident densities. 、
For example, the coefficient for unemployment rate in the final model is 0.254. The β̂ interpretation is that, holding the other variables constant, a one-percentage-point increase in the unemployment rate is associated with about a 0.254 percentage-point increase in predicted poverty rate. In terms of ŷ, if two otherwise similar tracts differ by one percentage point in unemployment, the model predicts the tract with higher unemployment to have a poverty rate about 0.254 percentage points higher.
The residual map shows that some spatial patterns remain, especially around Center City and North Philadelphia. One thing I would want to measure next is access to other neighborhood resources and services, such as transit, food stores, or community facilities. These data could come from Philadelphia’s open data portal or other city and regional open-data sources.
Finally, the last plot shows that low ACS CV does not necessarily mean a small prediction error. Some tracts with relatively reliable poverty estimates still have large residuals. This suggests that the remaining error is not simply caused by ACS sampling uncertainty; some of it likely reflects neighborhood characteristics that are not included in the model.

Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

  mutate(

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 5280/2) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate =  st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 153


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.
